title: Speed to Lead: Why the First Hour Wins Most Jobs | Halo Lead Exchange
h1: Speed to Lead: Why the First Hour Decides Most Home Improvement Jobs
metaDescription: A homeowner enquiry loses value by the hour. What the research says about response speed, and a simple first-hour routine any installer can run.
teaser: The enquiry you paid for is never warmer than the minute it arrives. Here is what the research says, and a first-hour routine that protects what you spend.
bodyHtml:
A homeowner fills in a form at 7.40pm because the problem is on their mind right now. Maybe a surveyor has just flagged the spray foam in their loft. Maybe the latest energy bill landed. Whatever prompted it, that moment is the warmest the enquiry will ever be. Every hour after it, the homeowner gets on with their evening, talks to someone else, or simply cools off.

That is why speed to lead matters more than almost any other habit in a trades business that buys enquiries. The lead does not lose its details over time. It loses its intent.

What the research actually says

The most quoted study on this is still a good one. Researchers writing in the Harvard Business Review in 2011 ("The Short Life of Online Sales Leads") audited how more than 2,000 US companies responded to web enquiries. Firms that tried to make contact within an hour were nearly seven times as likely to qualify the lead as firms that waited even an hour longer, and over 60 times as likely as firms that took a day or more. The average response time across the companies studied was around 42 hours.

It was not a study of UK installers, and nobody should pretend the multipliers transfer exactly. But the direction is hard to argue with, and anyone who has bought leads will recognise it: the homeowner you ring back in ten minutes talks to you properly. The one you ring back tomorrow lunchtime says "we have already had someone round".

Why homeowners go cold so quickly

  • They rarely ask just one firm. Comparing quotes is sensible, and the first credible voice usually sets the frame for everyone after.
  • The trigger fades. The worry that made them fill in the form is strongest on the day it happened.
  • Unknown numbers get ignored. A call that lands while the enquiry is fresh is recognisable. The same call two days later looks like a sales call.

A first-hour routine that works

None of this needs software. It needs a routine that someone actually owns:

  • Send new-lead notifications to a phone that is with a person, not to a shared inbox that gets checked at the end of the day.
  • Call within minutes if you possibly can. If you cannot answer the phone on a job, agree who in the business does.
  • If there is no answer, send a short text straight away saying who you are and why you are calling, then try again later the same day.
  • Spread your attempts: early evening often reaches people who were at work for the first call.
  • Write down what happened on each attempt. It stops the same homeowner being chased twice and tells you where leads are being lost.

Why this matters to how we run Lead Exchange

On Halo Lead Exchange, full contact details are released as soon as payment for a lead is confirmed, so nothing on our side should slow you down. We also ask buyers how quickly they contact new enquiries before we start working together, because a qualified lead that sits overnight is money half-wasted.

There is a practical reason too. A homeowner who simply does not answer is not, on its own, grounds for a replacement under our terms. A genuine enquiry that goes cold because nobody called for two days is not a bad lead. It is a slow response. The first-hour routine is the cheapest insurance you can buy on every lead you pay for.

If you want enquiries that are checked before they reach you, read how Halo Lead Exchange works, or apply to become a buyer.

faq.q: How quickly should I contact a new homeowner enquiry?
faq.a: As fast as you realistically can, ideally within minutes and certainly within the first hour. The evidence consistently shows the chance of a proper conversation drops sharply after that.

faq.q: What should I do if the homeowner does not answer?
faq.a: Send a short text immediately saying who you are and why you called, then try again later the same day and the following day at a different time. Record each attempt.

faq.q: Does speed still matter if a lead is exclusive to me?
faq.a: Yes. Exclusivity means no other installer is sent that enquiry by the supplier, but the homeowner may still be talking to firms they found elsewhere. Their interest also fades with time either way.

title: Exclusive vs Shared Leads: What You Pay For | Halo Lead Exchange
h1: Exclusive vs Shared Leads: What You Are Actually Paying For
metaDescription: Exclusive and shared homeowner leads are priced differently for a reason. How each works, which suits your business, and what to ask any lead supplier.
teaser: Exclusive leads cost more, shared leads cost less, and neither is automatically better. What matters is how many installers really get the enquiry, and whether the homeowner knows.
bodyHtml:
Almost every lead supplier offers some version of "exclusive" and "shared". The words sound simple. In practice they hide most of the questions that decide whether buying leads will pay for itself.

The basic difference

  • Exclusive: the supplier sends that homeowner enquiry to one installer only, usually for an agreed period. You are not racing another firm the supplier also sold it to.
  • Shared: the same enquiry goes to a small number of installers. Each pays less, and each is competing for the same job.

The price gap reflects the competition. A shared lead is cheaper because your realistic chance of winning it is lower. An exclusive lead is dearer because, if you respond well, the job is more likely to be yours.

Which suits your business?

A few honest questions settle it better than any sales pitch:

  • How fast do you respond? Shared leads reward the quickest credible callback. If you reliably call within minutes, shared can work. If calls go out the next day, you are mostly paying to come second.
  • What is your close rate? If you convert a high share of the homeowners you speak to, the extra cost of exclusivity is often worth it. If you are still refining your sales process, cheaper shared leads let you learn without overpaying.
  • How much capacity do you have? A supplier can only promise exclusivity in an area if the volume is there. If you want lots of enquiries, shared often gives you more of them.

The questions that matter more than the label

"Shared" can mean two installers or ten. "Exclusive" can mean exclusive for a day or for a month. Before you buy from anyone, ask:

  • Exactly how many installers can receive the same enquiry?
  • For how long is an exclusive lead exclusive?
  • Does the homeowner know their details may go to more than one business, and did they agree to that?
  • Is the enquiry matched to your service and area, or sent to everyone on the list?

That third question is the one most often skipped, and the one that causes most complaints. A homeowner who expected one callback and gets six feels misled, and that feeling lands on whichever installer rings last.

How Halo Lead Exchange handles it

On Lead Exchange, each buyer's arrangement is agreed with them before any leads are supplied, whether that is exclusive or shared. Enquiries are never broadcast to every installer we work with. They are matched by service, postcode coverage and capacity, and an enquiry only goes to more than one business where the homeowner has agreed to that.

It is a slower way to run a marketplace than selling every lead five times. It is also the only way we have found that keeps homeowners answering the phone. Read how Halo Lead Exchange works, or apply to become a buyer.

faq.q: Are exclusive leads always better than shared leads?
faq.a: No. Exclusive leads suit installers with a strong close rate and limited appetite for competition. Shared leads can be better value if you respond very quickly and want more volume.

faq.q: How many installers receive a shared lead?
faq.a: It varies by supplier, which is why you should always ask. On Halo Lead Exchange the arrangement is agreed with each buyer upfront and an enquiry only goes to more than one business where the homeowner has agreed.

faq.q: Does the homeowner know their enquiry is shared?
faq.a: They should. A reputable supplier records what the homeowner agreed to, including whether their details may be passed to more than one business.

title: Why You See a Redacted Lead Before Paying | Halo Lead Exchange
h1: Why You See a Redacted Preview Before You Pay for a Lead
metaDescription: Paying for a lead you have never seen is a gamble. Why Lead Exchange shows a redacted summary first, what it includes, and what stays hidden until payment.
teaser: You should not have to pay for an enquiry blind, and homeowners should not have their details sent to businesses that never commit. A redacted preview solves both.
bodyHtml:
A lot of lead buying works on trust in the wrong direction. You pay first, then find out whether the enquiry is in your area, for a job you do, from someone who actually owns the property. If it is not, you are into a replacement conversation for something you could have spotted in ten seconds.

Lead Exchange is built the other way round. Before you pay for anything, you see a redacted summary of the enquiry. You decide whether you want it. Only then does payment happen, and only after payment is confirmed are the homeowner's contact details released.

What the preview shows

The summary is designed to answer the question "is this a job for me?" without identifying anyone. Typically it includes:

  • The service needed, for example spray foam removal, solar and battery, or roofing.
  • The general area, such as the postcode district rather than the full address.
  • The kind of property and whether the homeowner has confirmed they own it.
  • Useful qualification details where we have them, such as timeframe and what prompted the enquiry.

What stays hidden until payment

The homeowner's name, phone number, email address and full address. Those are released once payment is confirmed, together with a reminder of how the details may be used.

Why it works this way

There are two reasons, and they protect two different people.

It protects you. You only pay for enquiries you have chosen, in places you cover, for work you do. The most common reasons a lead turns out to be useless are visible before you spend a penny.

It protects the homeowner. Their personal details are not sent to businesses that are only browsing. They go to the business that has committed to the enquiry, which is also exactly the kind of handling homeowners are entitled to expect under UK data protection law.

What happens after you say yes

You receive a secure payment link for the agreed price. Once payment is confirmed on our side, the full details are released to you, usually the same day. From that moment, speed matters: the sooner you call, the more the enquiry is worth.

It is a small extra step compared with buying leads blind, and it removes most of the arguments that make lead buying feel like a gamble. See how Halo Lead Exchange works, or apply to become a buyer.

faq.q: Can I see the homeowner's phone number before I pay?
faq.a: No. Contact details are released only after payment is confirmed. The redacted summary gives you enough to decide whether the job suits you without exposing the homeowner's personal data.

faq.q: How long does it take to receive full details after paying?
faq.a: Payment is checked on our side before release, and details are usually released the same day.

faq.q: What if the preview looked right but the lead turns out to be wrong?
faq.a: If the details are materially incorrect, the enquiry is a duplicate, or it fails the criteria agreed with you, that is what the replacement policy is for.

title: Pay Per Lead, Packages or Retainers? | Halo Lead Exchange
h1: Pay Per Lead, Prepaid Packages or Pay on Results: Choosing How You Pay for Leads
metaDescription: Pay per lead, prepaid credit packages, retainers and pay on results compared for installers, with a simple way to work out what each lead really costs you.
teaser: How you pay for leads shapes your cash flow, your risk and how hard the supplier works for you. The main models compared, and the one calculation that matters.
bodyHtml:
Most conversations about buying leads start with price per lead. The more useful question is how you pay, because the payment model decides who carries the risk, how predictable your costs are, and what the supplier is really being rewarded for.

Pay per lead

You pay for each enquiry individually, usually once you have chosen to take it. It is the simplest model and the lowest commitment: no upfront spend, no minimum volume, and you can stop at any time.

The trade-off is that it is usually the highest price per enquiry, and supply is not guaranteed. It suits installers who are testing a new area or a new supplier, or who only want work occasionally.

Prepaid packages and credits

You buy a bundle of leads, or credits, in advance. In return you usually get a lower price per lead and a supplier who is committed to delivering a set number of enquiries.

The risk shifts towards you: you have paid before seeing the leads. That is why it matters what happens if a lead in the package turns out to be bad. Packages suit installers who already know they can convert enquiries from that supplier and want predictable volume.

Trials

A small paid trial covering the first few leads is a sensible middle ground. You get real enquiries and see how you convert them before committing to a bigger package, and the supplier gets enough commitment to treat you as a serious buyer.

Monthly retainers

Common with marketing agencies: a fixed monthly fee for running campaigns on your behalf, whatever the results. It can work with an agency you trust, but you are paying for activity rather than enquiries, and the lead volume each month can vary a lot.

Pay on results

Paying only when a lead becomes a job sounds ideal. It is rarely offered, for understandable reasons: the supplier carries all the cost of finding the homeowner, has no control over how quickly or well the enquiry is followed up, and has to rely on the installer to report which jobs were won. Where it exists it tends to be priced high to cover that risk, and it needs a lot of trust on both sides.

The calculation that matters

Whatever the model, work out your cost per won job, not your cost per lead:

Cost per job = price per lead ÷ your close rate.

As an illustration only: if a lead costs £50 and you win one job in every five leads, each job has cost you £250 in leads. If you win one in three, it is about £167. Compare that with the margin on a typical job and the right price per lead becomes obvious. It also shows why speed and follow-up matter so much: improving your close rate lowers your real cost without the supplier changing anything.

How Halo Lead Exchange charges

Lead Exchange works on pay per lead and on prepaid packages, with terms agreed with each buyer before anything is supplied. Payment is made through a secure payment link, and a lead's full contact details are released once payment is confirmed. There is no monthly retainer and no fee for leads you choose not to take.

If you want to talk through which model fits your business, read how Halo Lead Exchange works, or apply to become a buyer.

faq.q: What is the cheapest way to buy leads?
faq.a: Prepaid packages usually have the lowest price per lead, but the cheapest option is whichever gives you the lowest cost per won job. That depends on your close rate as much as on the price.

faq.q: Should I start with a package or pay per lead?
faq.a: If you have never bought from a supplier before, start with pay per lead or a small trial. Move to a package once you know you can convert their enquiries.

faq.q: Do you charge a monthly fee?
faq.a: Halo Lead Exchange does not charge a monthly retainer. You pay per lead or for an agreed package, and only for leads you choose to take.

title: Why Every Homeowner Enquiry Is Qualified | Halo Lead Exchange
h1: Why Every Homeowner Enquiry Is Qualified Before It Reaches an Installer
metaDescription: A raw form fill is not a lead. What qualifying a homeowner enquiry involves, why it matters to the installer paying for it, and what it cannot guarantee.
teaser: Anyone can sell you form fills. What separates a lead worth paying for is the checking that happens before it reaches you, and being honest about what checking cannot promise.
bodyHtml:
An advert can produce a lot of form fills very cheaply. Some are genuine homeowners with a real job. Some are tenants who cannot commission work. Some are curious, some typed the wrong number, and some are the same person submitting twice. If all of them are passed straight to an installer, the installer pays for the sorting.

Qualification is the work of sorting them before they reach you. It is the main thing you are paying a lead supplier for, and the thing most worth asking about.

What we check

  • Ownership. Whether the person confirms they own the property. A tenant usually cannot authorise work like spray foam removal, however interested they are.
  • The job. Whether the service they need is one the matched installer actually does.
  • The area. Whether the postcode sits inside a buyer's agreed coverage.
  • The timeframe and reason. Whether they are ready to go or still researching, so you know how to approach the call.
  • The contact details. Whether the phone number and email look valid, and that it is not a duplicate of an enquiry we already have.

When an enquiry arrives incomplete

Some enquiries, particularly from short social media forms, arrive with only a name, number and postcode. Rather than throw those away or pass them on half-finished, we hold them back and ask the homeowner to complete the missing details first. An enquiry that does not meet the standard is flagged for manual review instead of being sold.

What qualification cannot do

It is worth being honest here. Qualification can confirm that a homeowner is real, owns the property, needs the work and is in your area. It cannot promise they will buy from you. They may get several quotes, decide to wait, or go with someone they already know.

That is why a good replacement policy covers leads that are genuinely wrong, such as incorrect details, duplicates or enquiries outside the agreed criteria, but not homeowners who simply chose not to go ahead. A supplier who promises otherwise is promising something nobody can deliver.

Why we bother

Because the alternative is a marketplace where installers stop trusting the leads, stop calling quickly, and stop buying. Every enquiry that reaches a Lead Exchange buyer has been checked against the criteria agreed with that buyer, so the time you spend on the phone goes on homeowners worth talking to.

See how Halo Lead Exchange works, or apply to become a buyer.

faq.q: What makes a homeowner lead qualified?
faq.a: At minimum: a real homeowner who owns the property, needs the specific service, is inside your coverage area, and has given valid contact details. Timeframe and reason for the enquiry help you prioritise.

faq.q: Does a qualified lead guarantee a job?
faq.a: No. Qualification confirms the enquiry is genuine and relevant. Whether it becomes a job depends on the homeowner's decision and on how quickly and well the installer follows up.

faq.q: What happens to incomplete enquiries?
faq.a: They are not passed on as they are. The homeowner is asked to complete the missing details, and enquiries that do not meet the standard are flagged for manual review.

title: Homeowner Consent and Buying Leads | Halo Lead Exchange
h1: Homeowner Consent and Lead Buying: What Installers Should Expect From a Supplier
metaDescription: Buying leads means handling homeowners' personal data. What a supplier should record about consent, why it protects you, and the rules buyers should follow.
teaser: When you buy a lead, you take on responsibility for someone's personal details. The consent behind that lead protects you as much as the homeowner.
bodyHtml:
Every homeowner lead contains personal data: a name, a phone number, an address. When you buy it, you become responsible for how that data is used. Most installers never think about this until a homeowner asks the awkward question: "How did you get my number?"

The answer to that question is the consent the homeowner gave when they made the enquiry. A good supplier can show you exactly what it was. A poor one cannot.

This guide is general information, not legal advice. UK GDPR and the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations set the rules; if you are unsure how they apply to your business, take proper advice.

What a supplier should be able to tell you

  • What the homeowner agreed to. The actual wording they saw, not a summary.
  • When they agreed. A record tied to the enquiry, so it can be produced if anyone asks.
  • Who their details could go to. Whether it is a named business or a described category, such as approved spray foam removal installers, and whether it could be more than one.
  • What they did not agree to. Agreeing to be contacted about an enquiry is not agreeing to join a marketing list.

Why it protects you

If a homeowner complains, the installer who called them is usually the one they complain to. Being able to say "you asked for a quote through this service on this date, and agreed to be put in touch with installers like us" ends most of those conversations. Not being able to say it can turn one complaint into a reputation problem.

How Lead Exchange handles consent

We record the consent wording each homeowner was shown, and which version, against their enquiry. Before a homeowner is introduced to a particular business, that introduction is confirmed for that enquiry. A yes for one installer is never treated as a yes for another. Homeowners are never added to marketing lists through Lead Exchange.

What we ask of buyers

Buying a lead comes with a few simple obligations, set out in our buyer terms:

  • Contact the homeowner only about the enquiry you bought.
  • Do not pass their details to anyone else.
  • Do not add them to marketing lists or send them unrelated marketing without their separate consent.
  • Tell us within 48 hours if a homeowner complains or asks how you got their details.

None of it is complicated, and all of it is what keeps homeowners willing to make enquiries in the first place. Read our buyer terms, see how Halo Lead Exchange works, or apply to become a buyer.

faq.q: Can I add homeowners from purchased leads to my mailing list?
faq.a: Not on the strength of the lead alone. The homeowner agreed to be contacted about their enquiry, not to receive marketing. Lead Exchange buyer terms do not allow it.

faq.q: What should I say if a homeowner asks how I got their number?
faq.a: Explain that they made an enquiry through Halo Lead Exchange and agreed to be put in touch with a suitable installer. Then let us know within 48 hours so we can follow up.

faq.q: Is this legal advice?
faq.a: No. It is general information about good practice. For advice on your own obligations under UK GDPR and PECR, speak to a qualified adviser.

title: What Counts as a Bad Lead? Fair Replacements | Halo Lead Exchange
h1: What Counts as a Bad Lead, and How a Fair Replacement Policy Should Work
metaDescription: Wrong numbers, duplicates and leads outside your criteria deserve a replacement. A homeowner who chose another installer does not. How a fair policy draws the line.
teaser: Every lead buyer eventually gets one that goes nowhere. Whether that is a bad lead or just business depends on a line a good supplier draws clearly, in writing, before you buy.
bodyHtml:
Buy enough leads and some will go nowhere. The question that decides whether a supplier relationship lasts is what happens next, and whether both sides agreed on the answer before any money changed hands.

What genuinely counts as a bad lead

A fair replacement policy covers enquiries that were wrong when you received them:

  • Materially incorrect contact details. The number does not connect or belongs to someone else, and there is no working way to reach the homeowner.
  • Duplicates. You have been sold the same enquiry twice within the agreed period.
  • Enquiries outside the agreed criteria. For example, outside your coverage area, for a service you do not offer, or from someone who turns out not to own the property when ownership was part of what you agreed.

What does not count

Just as important, and where most disagreements start:

  • The homeowner did not answer, or has not called back yet.
  • The homeowner chose another installer.
  • You quoted and they decided not to go ahead, or to wait.

These are the normal outcomes of a genuine enquiry. A supplier who refunds every lead that does not turn into a job either charges a lot more for every lead to cover it, or will not be around for long.

Time limits and evidence

A fair policy also sets a clear window for raising a problem, and asks for reasonable evidence. Lead Exchange's standard terms give buyers three calendar days from receiving a lead's full details to raise a replacement request; the exact terms that apply to your industry are set out in the published policy. A short window keeps the process honest: problems with a lead's details are obvious within a day or two of calling.

Why the policy should be published before you buy

If the rules only appear after a lead goes wrong, you are negotiating from a weak position. A supplier confident in its leads will show you the policy upfront, written down, before you pay for anything.

Lead Exchange publishes its policies: the Spray Foam Removal Refund and Replacement Policy, and the Lead Replacement Policy for Solar & Battery and Roofing. Read them before you buy, then see how Halo Lead Exchange works or apply to become a buyer.

faq.q: Is a homeowner who does not answer a bad lead?
faq.a: No. Not answering is a normal part of following up a genuine enquiry. Keep trying at different times of day, and send a text explaining who you are.

faq.q: How long do I have to report a bad lead?
faq.a: Under Lead Exchange's standard terms, three calendar days from receiving the full details. Check the published policy for your industry for the exact terms.

faq.q: Do I get a refund or a replacement?
faq.a: That depends on the published policy for your industry. Replacement leads are the usual remedy for a lead that is genuinely wrong.
